record.paper_title: NTN-based 6G Localization: Vision, Role of LEOs, and Open Problems
record.original_question: When a low-earth-orbit (LEO) satellite has unused communication beams, how should 6G non-terrestrial-network (NTN) positioning schedule and control spare beams to transmit low-signal-to-noise-ratio-decodable positioning reference signals (PRS) outside the satellite's normal beam coverage, such as when the satellite is passing over a land-ocean boundary?

evidence.quote: Spare Beams. Since PRS is designed to be decoded at very low SNR, the satellites may use spare beams to transmit PRS to locations outside its beam coverage. These spare beams can be activated opportunistically when the satellite has less ground area to cover (e.g., the LEO is passing over a land-ocean boundary).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a low-earth-orbit (LEO) satellite equipped with a phased-array antenna capable of forming up to B simultaneous directional beams. At any time t, let C(t) ⊆ {1,…,B} denote the subset of beams currently allocated to communication services within the satellite's nominal ground footprint, and let S(t) = {1,…,B} \ C(t) be the set of currently unused ("spare") beams. The satellite's nominal coverage cell N(t) ⊂ R^2 on the Earth's surface may shrink (for instance, when the satellite passes over a land–ocean boundary, so that the portion of N(t) over land is much smaller than over the ocean), leaving |S(t)| > 0.

Positioning reference signals (PRS) are broadcast waveforms designed so that user equipment (UE) located in a region R can estimate its position by combining time-of-arrival or carrier-phase measurements from multiple satellites. PRS waveforms are decodable at very low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), so a satellite may steer a spare beam from S(t) to illuminate a target ground region T(t) ⊂ R^2 located outside N(t).

Let U(t) ⊂ R^2 denote the set of UEs requesting positioning service at time t. For each UE u ∈ U(t), positioning accuracy depends on the geometric dilution of precision (GDOP) determined by the set of visible satellites currently transmitting PRS toward u, on the per-link SNR (which depends on beam direction, off-boresight angle, atmospheric attenuation, and slant range), and on the PRS bandwidth and integration time.

Design and analyze an opportunistic spare-beam scheduling and beam-pointing policy π that, given the satellite ephemerides, the time-varying spare-beam sets S(t), the spatial distribution of UEs U(t), and the communication-service constraints (so that beams allocated to C(t) are never preempted), assigns to each spare beam in S(t) a pointing direction (i.e. a target region T(t)) and a PRS transmission schedule, with the objectives:

(i) maximizing the expected positioning accuracy (e.g. minimizing the time- and UE-averaged position-error bound, or equivalently maximizing a Fisher-information-based utility) for UEs outside the nominal coverage N(t);
(ii) guaranteeing prescribed PRS coverage and revisit-time bounds at each location in a service area of interest; and
(iii) respecting hardware constraints, including total radiated power, beam-switching latency, and inter-beam interference.

Specifically: (a) formulate this spare-beam PRS scheduling problem as a mathematical optimization (e.g. a mixed-integer or stochastic optimal-control problem), (b) characterize its computational complexity, and (c) provide a policy with provable performance guarantees relative to the offline optimum, or establish fundamental performance limits.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in a forward-looking vision paper on 6G non-terrestrial-network localization. A web search did not surface any subsequent work that formally formulates or solves the opportunistic spare-beam PRS scheduling problem for LEO satellites with provable guarantees. The problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.snippet: Listed among open problems for 6G NTN localization, including opportunistic spare-beam PRS transmission outside nominal coverage.
status_evidence.claim: The opportunistic spare-beam PRS scheduling question is explicitly raised as an open research direction.
